title: Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers: evolution, translational applications and clinical considerations

# Hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers: evolution, translational applications and clinical considerations

PMC13678070. Frontiers in Medicine, 13:1939029. Published 2026-10-05.

## Authors

Huan Tang, Xinyi Liu, Hai Zhang, Xiaobo Huang, Chun Pan, Lin Chen

## Details

- DOI: https://doi.org/10.3389/fmed.2026.1939029
- PMID: 42898493 (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42898493/)
- PMCID: PMC13678070
- License: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

---

## Abstract

Tissue survival depends on adequate oxygen delivery, yet when red blood cell (RBC) transfusions are unavailable or contraindicated, restoring oxygen delivery remains an urgent clinical need. To meet this need, researchers have developed hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs) that transport oxygen via cell-free hemoglobin circulating in plasma. However, the intrinsic toxicity of cell-free hemoglobin (Hb) has slowed its clinical translation. More fundamentally, it has shifted the field's focus from universal blood substitutes toward indication-specific solutions. Despite persistent mitigation efforts, no HBOC has gained full Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for human use, suggesting that these toxicities are not tractable engineering problems but intrinsic liabilities of the cell-free Hb molecule. A meta-analysis of early clinical trials reported increased risks of death and myocardial infarction with several HBOCs, prompting a clinical hold on HBOC trials in the United States. In this review, we trace the evolution of engineering strategies and examine the functional mechanisms that underpin these approaches. We then evaluate HBOCs not as universal RBC substitutes but as context-dependent strategies for oxygen delivery across acute resuscitation, organ preservation, and hypoxia-driven pathologies, followed by a safety assessment. In each scenario, clinical value rests on providing temporary oxygen support when standard transfusion is unavailable or inadequate, rather than on replicating the full functionality of RBCs. Although a universal RBC substitute remains a distant goal, HBOCs are progressively evolving into oxygen therapeutics specific to indications. Their clinical adoption will require rigorous evidence of long-term safety, manufacturing reproducibility, and clinically meaningful efficacy in well-defined patient populations.

## Introduction

Adequate oxygen supply is the prerequisite for cell metabolism and organ function (1). In vertebrates, red blood cells (RBCs) serve as the main carriers of oxygen throughout the body (2). Within RBCs, hemoglobin (Hb), a tetrameric heme protein whose ferrous iron (Fe²⁺) reversibly binds oxygen, is packed at high intracellular concentration and thereby provides a large oxygen-carrying capacity. Its cooperative binding and allosteric regulation enable efficient oxygen loading in the lungs and controlled release in the microcirculation (3). When the total number of RBCs in circulation is seriously insufficient, restoring oxygen-carrying capacity through allogeneic blood transfusion remains a life-saving intervention (4).

Therefore, blood transfusion is an essential therapeutic intervention in contemporary clinical practice. However, its availability is often constrained by donor shortages, limited storage duration, cold-chain requirements, blood-group compatibility (5). Transfusion also carries risks including transfusion-related complications (6). These limitations are particularly pronounced during mass-casualty incidents, military operations, natural disasters, pandemics, as well as in remote or resource-limited environments, where timely access to compatible blood products is frequently compromised (7, 8).

These challenges have drawn sustained attention to alternative strategies to maintain tissue oxygenation when RBC transfusion is impossible (9). Among these, hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs) have been extensively researched because Hb, as a natural oxygen binding protein in RBCs, can facilitate immediate oxygen transport and is not limited by blood type matching or the storage limitations of donor blood (10). However, a meta-analysis of 16 randomized trials reported increased risks of death and myocardial infarction with several HBOCs (11), and no HBOC has since gained the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for human use (12). Early cell-free Hb preparations and a number of chemically modified products were associated with vasoconstriction, hypertension, and oxidative tissue damage (13). These adverse reactions mainly arise from the ability of extracellular Hb to remove nitric oxide (NO), undergo autoxidation, generate methemoglobin (MetHb), and destroy endothelial homeostasis (14–16). These findings have shifted the field's research from empirical Hb stabilization to mechanism-based design. This approach integrates protein engineering, polymer chemistry and materials science to improve both oxygen supply capacity and biocompatibility simultaneously.

Various chemical and macromolecular domains, including polymer coupling, polymerization, and cross-linking, have been used to increase the molecular size of HBOCs. These approaches have been implemented to prolong the circulatory half-life and reduce renal clearance of HBOCs. Surface engineering methods, including polydopamine coatings and metal-phenolic networks (MPNs), have been investigated for their potential to impart antioxidant and endothelial-protective properties (17, 18). At the molecular level, rational protein design has also been applied. A notable example is the β-F41K mutation (β-chain phenylalanine-to-lysine substitution at position 41), designed to stabilize the heme microenvironment, preserve redox homeostasis, and limit cofactor loss (19). Concurrently, nanostructured encapsulation systems, such as zeolitic imidazolate framework-8 (ZIF-8) scaffolds, lipid vesicles, and polymeric microgels, generate biomimetic microenvironments that potentially enhance Hb stability, restrict direct plasma exposure, and facilitate more tightly regulated oxygen release (20–22). Collectively, these strategies represent a shift from chemically stabilized Hb solutions toward more physiologically integrated oxygen-delivery systems.

The level of translational evidence varies widely among HBOC platforms. Cross-linked and polymerized Hb (e.g., diaspirin cross-linked and glutaraldehyde-polymerized products) have reached phase II/III clinical trials (23, 24), as have selected PEGylated Hb products (25). In contrast, most encapsulation-based systems, including liposomal, microgel, and framework-based carriers, have only undergone in vitro characterization and preclinical testing (26). Therefore, it is essential to distinguish among these levels of evidence, which include clinically validated efficacy, in vivo data, experimentally confirmed mechanisms, and unverified applications.

Although there have been several reviews of the engineering design of HBOCs (27–29), most of the existing studies discuss a single platform in isolation, rather than incorporating it into a maturity-based framework for systematic synthesis. In this review, we divide HBOC-related strategies into three levels: (i) products that have entered early clinical trials or obtained compassionate use authorization; (ii) preclinical research platforms that have passed in vivo proof of concept; and (iii) exploratory biological materials at the in vitro characterization stage. For each level, we evaluate the safety and efficacy of different design strategies. Here, efficacy is defined according to the evidentiary tier: clinical outcomes for products in clinical trials, in vivo oxygen-delivery performance for preclinical platforms, and in vitro oxygen-binding and release properties for exploratory materials. We further weigh the proposed mechanisms according to the rigor of the supporting evidence, to distinguish between the function that has been clinically verified and the function that is still in the experimental research stage.

We propose the concept of the “oxygen bridge”, a carrier that temporarily sustains tissue oxygenation when the body's own oxygen-carrying capacity is impaired, and with a role that varies across clinical contexts. Our concern is not whether these oxygen carrier preparations can replicate the function of RBCs, but whether they can provide effective temporary oxygen supply when blood transfusion is unavailable or inadequate.

## Literature search strategy

This narrative review was conducted using a structured search of PubMed, Web of Science, Scopus, and Google Scholar, for the period from January 2000 to December 2025; the search was last updated in February 2026. Landmark studies published before 2000 were included if they provided foundational clinical evidence. The search strategy was designed to cover the following areas: the concept of blood substitutes, toxicity mechanisms, translational applications, and the historical development of HBOCs. Disagreements regarding inclusion criteria or evidence classification were discussed until consensus was reached. Non-English literature, conference abstracts lacking sufficient methodological detail, editorials, and research not directly related to HBOC formulation, function, safety, or clinical translation were excluded from the analysis.

## The evolution and historical development of HBOCs

### Overview of historical evolution

Research on artificial blood substitutes can be traced back to the early 20th century and was driven by the urgent need for alternatives to donated blood. Typical application scenarios include trauma resuscitation and combat casualty care (30). From this need, two main technical routes emerged. Early research focused on perfluorocarbon (PFC) emulsions, which carry oxygen through physical dissolution. Subsequent research focused on HBOCs, which are designed to mimic the oxygen-binding and release characteristics of natural RBCs (31–33). Although PFC emulsions have high oxygen solubility, their volatility, emulsion instability, and limited biocompatibility have hindered their widespread clinical application (34).

The first generation of HBOCs was composed of chemically stabilized cell-free Hb. Although these compounds entered the clinical trial, their application was eventually limited by toxicity, mainly due to NO scavenging and oxidative instability (23, 35, 36). These findings prompted researchers to shift their focus from empirical chemical modification toward mechanism-based design strategies. In these mechanistic studies, molecular size was a key parameter, because smaller Hb species can cross the vascular endothelium and scavenge NO (37). Unmodified cell-free Hb (∼64 kDa) dissociates rapidly into αβ dimers and is cleared by the kidneys, resulting in a very short circulatory half-life. Its small size allows Hb to enter the the subendothelial space, where it can scavenge NO and cause vasoconstriction (38). To address these limitations, subsequent HBOC designs employed polymer chemistry, protein engineering, and nanoscale encapsulation technology (18, 20). These modifications increased the hydrodynamic radius and molecular weight of the constructs, thereby prolonging intravascular residence time and reducing endothelial extravasation. However, merely increasing molecular size did not eliminate HBOC-associated toxicity. The degree to which these strategies mitigate NO scavenging, oxidative stress, and resulting vascular side effects; further preclinical and clinical validation is therefore needed (39). Therefore, molecular size should be considered part of a broader safety and efficacy strategy rather than a standalone solution.
